newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Scottish nationalists poised for poll push.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Scottish nationalists poised for poll push.

text.p: Their annual conference may have been overshadowed by a row over "Nazi" slurs, but Scottish nationalists insist they are in better shape than ever to make a difference in Scotland as elections near.

After the 72 Scottish National Party (SNP) parliamentary candidates were introduced on stage to delegates assembled in Inverness, party leader Alex Salmond recalled the historic words of the Duke of Wellington reviewing his Highland troops.
"I don't know what they'll do to the enemy, but by God they frighten me."
The enemy for the "Bravehearts" in the SNP is the opposition Labour Party, the biggest party in Scotland and well ahead of the ruling Conservatives in British opinion polls.
With a general election due by next May, the SNP enjoys nearly 30 percent support in Scotland, while Labour stands at 48 percent and the Conservatives are running third at about 15.
Labour has been severely damaged in Scotland by a series of policy switches on its plans for a referendum on a devolved Scottish parliament.
The Scot Nats, as they are called, are in much better shape than fellow Celtic fringe nationalists in Wales, who can only muster 16 percent of voter support.

With campaign funds approaching 500,000 pounds ($780,000), five times what he was able to spend at the last election in 1992, Salmond is determined that his party can mount its most credible challenge yet.
The SNP has four members of parliament in London, and while its electoral support is spread widely across Scotland, a big push in some key constituencies could reap major dividends.
A large increase in the number of SNP members of parliament at the next election could force the next government, probably Labour, to put Scottish affairs near the top of its agenda.
After a series of changes of mind, Labour now proposes a two-question referendum on devolution, asking for separate approval for a parliament and for tax-raising powers.
The Conservatives remain committed to the union of Scotland with England which has endured since 1707.
The SNP must overcome some serious presentational problems before it can even come close to ending the link with the "auld enemy".

Carefully laid plans to set out a reasoned economic case for Scottish independence were derailed at the SNP conference when a top party figure compared Labour's Scottish affairs spokesman to the World War Two Nazi collaborator known as Lord Haw Haw.
The attack, by SNP policy chief Alex Neil, drew an ovation from party faithful but caused a huge row with Labour, which his resignation. Salmond forced Neil to apologise.

The affair dominated media coverage of the conference and led to suspicions that Neil's comments were not so much a joke that misfired as an attempt to upstage SNP treasury spokesman John Swinney's economic presentation.
Neil, according to some commentators, was positioning himself for a run at the party deputy leadership, a post Swinney would also contest.

Salmond's attempts to show that an independent Scotland would match the strong growth rates enjoyed by Ireland and become Europe's "tiger" economy could not compete, in news terms, with the "Nazi" row.
It was not the first time the SNP had been blown off course by an unfortunate remark by Neil.
In 1991 he embarrassed party leaders with the slogan "Scotland Free by 93". Now the party keeps quiet about when Scotland might become independent.
Salmond, meanwhile, has been consolidating his grip on the party, following the election to the national executive of several of his allies.
The 41-year-old economist has been trying to move the party away from simply blaming the English for Scotland's troubles by presenting a more positive brand of nationalism.
"The condition of Scotland is the inescapable responsibility of every adult Scot because we alone have the solution in our own hands," Salmond said.
The SNP says an independent Scotland would be the 21st richest nation in the world and has sought to dispel what it sees as the myth that Scotland is heavily subsidised by the government in London.
"The central argument of the SNP is that because Scotland is part of the union we do not achieve our full economic potential," Salmond said.
"We are constrained by policies which are inappropriate for Scotland and directly harm our people and our prosperity."

The party maintains that since the Conservatives came to power in 1979, $160 billion worth of North Sea oil and gas revenues have been "squandered" by London and oil could form a springboard for an independent Scottish economy.
Labour accuses the SNP of living in "wonderland", while the Conservatives say the nationalists would turn Scotland into "a backwater socialist state".
But the SNP may have found a vote-winner to confound its rivals. The nationalists plan to cut the price of whisky.
